questions.stem: Which type of business is owned by one person who has unlimited liability for all of its debts?
options: a private limited company
a public listed company
a government business enterprise
a sole trader
questions.explanation: A sole trader is owned and run by one person, and the business is not a separate legal entity, so the owner is personally liable for all its debts. Companies, whether private or public, give their shareholders limited liability.

questions.stem: A key feature of a public listed company is that:
options: it may have no more than fifty shareholders who are not employees
its shares can be bought and sold by the public on a stock exchange
its owners are personally liable for all of the debts of the business
it is owned by government and run commercially to make a profit
questions.explanation: A public listed company is listed on a stock exchange such as the ASX, so members of the public can buy and sell its shares. A limit of fifty non-employee shareholders applies to a private limited company, and government ownership describes a government business enterprise.

questions.stem: Mira and Josh run a Bendigo landscaping business together under a written agreement. They share the profits equally and each is personally liable for all of the business's debts. Their business is a:
options: social enterprise
partnership
sole trader
private limited company
questions.explanation: Two or more owners who share profits and carry unlimited liability for the business's debts form a partnership, usually set out in a partnership agreement. A private limited company would give them limited liability, and a sole trader has only one owner.

questions.stem: Coastline Pty Ltd is a family-owned company in Torquay. Compared with operating as a sole trader, a key advantage for its owners is that:
options: their personal assets are protected by limited liability
it can raise capital by selling shares to the general public on the ASX
the business ends automatically if one of the owners dies
it does not have to register with any government body
questions.explanation: A private limited company is a separate legal entity, so shareholders can lose only what they have invested and their personal assets are protected. A Pty Ltd company cannot offer shares to the public, must be registered with ASIC, and continues to exist when an owner dies.

questions.stem: A social enterprise is best described as a business that:
options: relies only on donations and government grants for income and does not sell anything
sells shares to the public on the ASX to fund a range of community projects
trades to meet a social or environmental need, reinvesting most profits in it
is owned by government and run commercially to earn a profit for the state
questions.explanation: A social enterprise earns its income through trade, like any business, but exists mainly to meet a social or environmental need and puts most of its profit back into that mission. A body funded only by donations is a charity rather than a trading business.

questions.stem: A government business enterprise (GBE) is:
options: a privately owned company that wins government contracts to deliver public services
a government department funded fully by taxes that sells nothing to customers
a social enterprise funded by government grants to meet a community need
a government-owned business that trades commercially and aims to make a profit
questions.explanation: A GBE is owned by a level of government but is run like a business, selling goods or services and aiming to make a profit. A private contractor is privately owned, and a tax-funded department does not trade commercially.

questions.stem: Kaur Electrical is a sole trader in Geelong. The owner is considering converting it to a private limited company. Which is a disadvantage of making this change?
options: the business will no longer be able to borrow money from a bank
it must meet more complex registration and reporting requirements
the owner will become personally liable for all of the company's debts
the owner can no longer receive any share of the business's profits
questions.explanation: Companies must register with ASIC and meet ongoing reporting and legal obligations, which add cost and complexity compared with a sole trader. The change would give the owner limited liability, not unlimited, and a company can still borrow and pay its owners from profits.

questions.stem: Which comparison of a general partnership and a public listed company is correct?
options: the partnership can raise capital by selling shares on the ASX, while the company cannot
the company has no reporting obligations to its shareholders, while the partnership does
shareholders in the company have limited liability, while the partners have unlimited liability
both are separate legal entities from their owners, so each can sue and be sued in its own legal name
questions.explanation: In a general partnership the partners are personally liable for its debts, while a company's shareholders can lose only their investment. A partnership is not a separate legal entity and cannot list on the ASX, and a public listed company has strict reporting obligations.

questions.stem: Pantry Fresh, a grocery chain in Geelong, sets a target of raising its sales from 12 per cent to 15 per cent of all grocery sales in its region. This objective is to:
options: increase market share
improve efficiency
fulfil a social need
meet shareholder expectations
questions.explanation: Market share is a business's sales as a proportion of total sales in its market, so a target of moving from 12 to 15 per cent of regional grocery sales is an objective to increase market share. Efficiency concerns how well resources are used, not the share of the market won.

questions.stem: The business objective of improving efficiency refers to:
options: increasing the business's share of total sales in its industry
satisfying a customer want that no other business is meeting
making the best use of resources to produce goods and services
the degree to which the business achieves its stated objectives
questions.explanation: Efficiency is about how well a business uses its resources, producing more output or the same output at lower cost. The degree to which objectives are achieved is effectiveness, which students often confuse with efficiency.

questions.stem: Bayside Bikes set a target of 500 bike services in March and completed 510, but it needed 30 per cent more staff hours than it had planned. In March the business was:
options: neither efficient nor effective
effective but not efficient
efficient but not effective
both efficient and effective
questions.explanation: Bayside Bikes met its objective of 500 services, so it was effective. It used far more labour than planned to do so, which is a poor use of resources, so it was not efficient.

questions.stem: A café in Ballarat employs young people leaving homelessness, trains them as baristas and puts its profits into the training program. Its main objective is to:
options: increase market share
meet shareholder expectations
fulfil a social need
fulfil a market need
questions.explanation: The café exists mainly to help disadvantaged young people into work, which is a social need, and its profits are directed to that purpose. A market need is a want customers have for a product, which is not the main aim described.

questions.stem: A Toowoomba business begins selling gourmet dog treats after its research shows strong demand from local pet owners that no other retailer is meeting. This most directly fulfils:
options: a market need
a social need
an efficiency objective
shareholder expectations
questions.explanation: Providing a product that customers want and that is not already supplied fulfils a market need. A social need relates to improving the wellbeing of society or a disadvantaged group, which gourmet pet treats do not address.

questions.stem: Which business objective is most directly concerned with providing dividends and growth in the value of shares?
options: meeting shareholder expectations
fulfilling a market need
improving effectiveness
fulfilling a social or community need
questions.explanation: Shareholders expect a return on their investment, through dividends and a rising share value, so this objective is to meet shareholder expectations. Effectiveness is the degree to which a business achieves whatever objectives it has set.

questions.stem: Which stakeholder group's main interests in a business are usually fair wages, job security and safe working conditions?
options: employees
owners
suppliers
customers
questions.explanation: Employees depend on the business for their income and wellbeing at work, so they want fair pay, secure jobs and a safe workplace. Owners are mainly interested in profit and the value of their investment.

questions.stem: The suppliers of a business are mainly interested in:
options: low prices and good-quality products
secure jobs and fair rates of pay
regular orders and prompt payment
dividends and growth in share value
questions.explanation: Suppliers sell inputs to a business, so they want ongoing orders and prompt payment. Low prices and quality products are the interests of customers.

questions.stem: As stakeholders, the managers of a business are mainly interested in:
options: low prices, product quality and good after-sales service
the business limiting noise and pollution in the local area
meeting targets, career progression and their own remuneration
being paid promptly for the inputs they deliver to the business
questions.explanation: Managers are judged on whether they meet the business's objectives, and they want to advance their careers and be well paid. Prompt payment for inputs is a supplier interest, and low prices and quality are customer interests.

questions.stem: The interests of the general community in a business typically include:
options: dividends, a rising share price and a strong net profit
steady orders, long-term contracts and prompt payment of invoices
promotion opportunities, higher salaries and bonuses
local jobs, protection of the environment and ethical behaviour
questions.explanation: The general community is affected by a business's presence, so it wants local employment, little harm to the environment and ethical conduct. Dividends and share price are owners' interests, and steady orders are suppliers' interests.

questions.stem: The owners of a cannery in Shepparton want to cut costs by replacing older machinery with automated lines that need far fewer workers. This is most likely to create a conflict between:
options: customers and suppliers
suppliers and the general community
customers and managers
owners and employees
questions.explanation: The owners want lower costs and higher profit, while employees want to keep their jobs, so automation that reduces staff numbers sets their interests against each other. Customers and suppliers are not the groups whose interests clash in this case.

questions.stem: Ridgeway Quarries plans to expand into nearby bushland to raise its output and profit. Local residents oppose the plan because of dust, noise and loss of habitat. Which statement best explains the conflict?
options: employees seek higher wages, while owners want to keep labour costs low
customers want lower prices, while suppliers want higher prices for inputs
managers want more authority, while owners want to keep control themselves
owners seek higher profit, while the community wants to protect its environment
questions.explanation: The owners' interest is profit from expansion, while the general community wants to protect the local environment and its quality of life. Nothing in the case concerns wages, prices or authority within the business.

questions.stem: Which pair of stakeholder interests is most likely to conflict?
options: employees seeking safe conditions and managers seeking fewer workplace accidents
suppliers seeking regular orders and managers seeking a reliable supply of inputs
owners seeking higher profits and managers seeking to meet their profit targets
customers seeking lower prices and owners seeking higher profit margins
questions.explanation: Lower prices for customers reduce the margin owners earn on each sale, so these interests pull in opposite directions. In each of the other pairs the two groups want compatible outcomes, such as safety for both employees and managers.

questions.stem: Management at a Perth logistics firm sets tighter delivery times to lift productivity. Drivers say the new times force them to speed and skip rest breaks. Which statement best describes this situation?
options: a conflict between suppliers' interest in payment and customers' interest in low prices
an example of the general community and owners sharing the same interest in profit
an example of laissez-faire management, as drivers decide their own delivery times
a conflict between managers' interest in meeting targets and employees' interest in safety
questions.explanation: Managers want to meet productivity targets, while employees want safe working conditions, so the tighter times create a conflict between the two groups. Management has set the times, so the drivers are not choosing them, which rules out a laissez-faire style.

questions.stem: Under an autocratic management style, the manager:
options: makes all decisions alone and issues instructions without consultation
makes the decisions and then tries to convince employees of their benefits
seeks employees' views before making the final decision themselves
shares decision-making with employees, who reach agreement as a group
questions.explanation: An autocratic manager makes decisions without input from employees, and communication flows one way, from the top down. A manager who explains the decision to win support is using the persuasive style.

questions.stem: Which management style involves the manager making the decision and then explaining its benefits to win employees' acceptance?
options: consultative
autocratic
participative
persuasive
questions.explanation: A persuasive manager still makes the decision alone but tries to sell it to employees by explaining why it is a good one. An autocratic manager simply issues the decision without trying to win acceptance, and a consultative manager seeks views before deciding.

questions.stem: The manager of a Wollongong call centre asks her team for ideas about new rosters, considers their suggestions and then decides the final roster herself. She is using the:
options: consultative style
participative style
persuasive style
laissez-faire style
questions.explanation: Seeking employees' input but keeping the final decision is the consultative style, with two-way communication. Under the participative style, the manager and employees would decide together rather than the manager deciding alone.

questions.stem: At a design studio in Fitzroy, the manager and staff discuss the options together and reach agreement as a group on how to restructure their workflow. This is the:
options: participative style
consultative style
laissez-faire style
persuasive style
questions.explanation: In the participative style, decision-making is shared and the group reaches a decision together, with the manager acting as a facilitator. In the consultative style the manager listens to staff but makes the final decision alone.

questions.stem: A team of highly qualified research scientists is given a broad goal and left to decide how and when to do the work. Their manager is rarely involved. This is the:
options: participative style
consultative style
autocratic style
laissez-faire style
questions.explanation: A laissez-faire manager sets broad goals and gives employees the freedom to make their own decisions, with little direction. In the participative style the manager stays closely involved, sharing decisions with the group.

questions.stem: A fire breaks out in a warehouse in Laverton and staff must be evacuated immediately. Which management style is most appropriate, and why?
options: participative, because staff will support a decision they help to make
consultative, because the manager should gather staff views before acting
laissez-faire, because experienced staff will know what to do themselves
autocratic, because there is no time to consult and staff need clear direction
questions.explanation: In an emergency there is no time to seek views, so an autocratic style that gives clear, immediate instructions is most appropriate. Consulting or sharing the decision would cause dangerous delays.

questions.stem: A manager wants to use a laissez-faire style with a new team of school-leavers in their first week on a food-processing line. Which factor most clearly makes this style inappropriate?
options: the manager's own preference for it
the size of the business
the location of the factory
the employees' lack of experience
questions.explanation: Laissez-faire suits highly skilled, experienced employees who can work without direction, so inexperienced new staff need closer guidance. The manager prefers this style, so preference supports it rather than ruling it out.

questions.stem: Although she leads an experienced team, a manager uses a consultative style because she is most comfortable gathering views while keeping the final say. Which factor is shaping her choice of style?
options: the time available
the experience of employees
manager preference
the nature of the task
questions.explanation: Her choice comes from her own comfort with keeping the final decision, which is manager preference. Her experienced team might suit a more participative or laissez-faire style, so their experience is not what is driving her choice.

questions.stem: With the same team, a manager uses a participative style to plan the staff social club but an autocratic style when enforcing safety procedures on a building site. Which factor best explains the difference?
options: the nature of the task
the experience of employees
manager preference
the size of the team
questions.explanation: The team and the manager are the same in both cases, so the difference comes from the task: safety rules must be followed exactly, while planning a social club suits shared decisions. Employee experience cannot explain it, because the employees do not change.

questions.stem: The management skill of delegation involves:
options: handing an employee the authority to do a task while the manager stays accountable
setting objectives for the business and deciding the strategies used to achieve them
identifying a problem, weighing up the options and choosing the best alternative
transferring information clearly between people inside and outside the business
questions.explanation: Delegation means passing the authority to carry out a task to an employee, although the manager is still accountable for the result. Setting objectives and strategies is planning, and choosing between alternatives is decision-making.

questions.stem: Which management skill involves setting objectives and deciding the strategies and resources needed to achieve them?
options: leadership
delegation
interpersonal
planning
questions.explanation: Planning is the skill of setting goals and working out how they will be achieved and what resources are needed. Leadership is about influencing and inspiring others to work towards those goals.

questions.stem: Interpersonal skills are best described as the ability to:
options: choose the best course of action from a range of possible alternatives
assign tasks to employees and give them authority to carry them out
relate to, interact with and build relationships with other people
influence and inspire others to work towards a vision for the business
questions.explanation: Interpersonal skills involve relating well to others, including empathy, tact and resolving conflict. Influencing others to work towards a vision is leadership, a separate skill students often merge with interpersonal skills.

questions.stem: The owner of a Townsville tour company inspires her staff with a clear vision of becoming the region's most sustainable operator, and her staff work enthusiastically towards it. She is showing strong:
options: decision-making
leadership
delegation
planning
questions.explanation: Leadership is the ability to influence and inspire others to work towards the business's goals, as she does by sharing a vision her staff commit to. Planning sets the objectives and strategies, but the case focuses on how she motivates people.

questions.stem: A manager identifies a falling-sales problem, lists several possible responses, weighs up the costs and benefits of each and then chooses one. Which management skill is she using?
options: communication
delegation
interpersonal
decision-making
questions.explanation: Decision-making is the process of identifying a problem, generating alternatives, evaluating them and selecting the best one. Delegation would mean handing the task to someone else, which she has not done.

questions.stem: A manager uses a laissez-faire style. Which management skill will she need to rely on most, and why?
options: decision-making, because she makes most of the decisions herself
planning, because she sets out exactly how each task is to be done
communication, because she gives each instruction in close detail
delegation, because the authority to make decisions is passed to employees
questions.explanation: Under laissez-faire, employees are given the authority to decide how work is done, so delegation is the key skill. Making the decisions herself or setting out every task in detail would describe an autocratic approach.

questions.stem: A participative manager needs strong interpersonal skills mainly because she must:
options: give employees full freedom with very little contact from management
convince employees to accept decisions that she has already made
build trust and work closely with employees to reach shared decisions
make all of the decisions herself without input from her employees
questions.explanation: The participative style depends on the manager and employees deciding together, which requires good relationships, trust and the ability to manage disagreement. Convincing staff to accept a decision already made describes the persuasive style.

questions.stem: Corporate culture is best defined as:
options: the range of products and services that a business offers to its customers
the shared values, beliefs and assumptions that shape behaviour in a business
the formal structure of reporting relationships between managers and employees
the laws that govern how a business must treat its employees and customers
questions.explanation: Corporate culture is the shared values and beliefs of the people in a business, shown in how they behave and do things. A reporting structure is the organisation chart, which can influence culture but is not culture itself.

questions.stem: Which is an example of official corporate culture?
options: the unwritten rule that no one questions the boss
values in the business's mission statement
the jokes staff tell about management at lunch
the habit of leaving work early on Fridays
questions.explanation: Official culture is the culture management formally states, through mission statements, policies, logos and dress codes. Habits, jokes and unwritten rules show the real culture, which is what actually happens.

questions.stem: Real corporate culture is best revealed by:
options: how employees actually behave and treat each other
the values the business states in its annual report
the business's logo, slogan and official colours
the dress code set out in the employee handbook
questions.explanation: Real culture is what actually happens in the workplace, seen in day-to-day behaviour, language and the way people are treated. Annual reports, logos and handbooks are formal statements that make up the official culture.

questions.stem: Southgate Insurance's mission statement says 'Our people come first', yet staff are routinely expected to work unpaid overtime and are rarely thanked. This shows:
options: a conflict between the business's suppliers and customers
a gap between the official and real corporate culture
a real culture that strongly matches the official culture
a laissez-faire management style being used by managers
questions.explanation: The mission statement is the official culture, while unpaid overtime and lack of recognition show the real culture, and the two do not match. A strong culture would have staff experiencing the stated values in practice.
